data.title: Onboarding and New Starters Targeted
data.summary: New employees, identified from public announcements, were approached with onboarding pretexts and complied — they had no basis for judging what is normal, and every incentive to be helpful.
data.description:
A new starter is the ideal target: publicly announced, unfamiliar with internal processes, unable to recognise the people contacting them, and anxious to make a good impression. An instruction from "IT" on day three is indistinguishable from the genuine ones they have been receiving all week.

The window is reliable because onboarding is genuinely a period of unusual requests — install this, authenticate here, confirm your details — so the attacker's request does not stand out.

Starters are also unlikely to challenge a senior name, and often unaware of the reporting route, so an attempt against them may go unreported even when it is noticed.
data.recommendation:
* Cover security on day one, before systems access: how IT will contact them, what will never be asked, and how to report.
* Verify any unexpected IT instruction through the manager or a published number, and tell starters that doing so is expected.
* Avoid publicly announcing new starters in roles with privileged access.
* Pair starters with a named contact for their first weeks who they can ask without embarrassment.
data.short_recommendation: Brief new starters on day one, and verify IT contact through the manager.
